general.title: General validation
general.intro: A shared foundation for every product — whatever the category.
general/general-zbuduj-minimalna-wersje-: Build the minimum version of the solution

General MVP validation consists of building the minimum version of the solution: delivering only the features needed to fulfil the main assumption, connecting the key parts so that the user can do the main action, and getting the MVP to a state in which the first recipients can use it. The next step is starting testing with users — defining a research group suitable for testing the solution, setting the study period, making the MVP available to the chosen group and observing how they use the product and what problems they run into.

general/general-zbierz-feedback.title: Collect feedback
general/general-zbierz-feedback.guide_bo: Next, feedback is collected: getting users' direct opinions about their experience with the MVP, consulting the solution with specialists and other experienced people, recording defects, difficulties and unclear parts, and noting users' expectations regarding core and additional features. The collected feedback is analyzed — assessing user satisfaction, analyzing the reported problems to find the most frequently recurring defects and barriers, checking which features users really need, and drawing the most important conclusions about what needs changing and what needs further checking.

The collected feedback is analyzed — assessing user satisfaction, analyzing the reported problems to find the most frequently recurring defects and barriers, checking which features users really need, and drawing the most important conclusions about what needs changing and what needs further checking. b2b.title: B2B
b2b.intro: A layer for selling to companies — MVP, a test with business customers, feedback.
b2b/b2b-zbuduj-minimalna-wersje-rozwiaza: Build the minimum version of the solution

1.1. Deliver the core features of the MVP
Open the findings on the scope of the first version intended for business customers. Focus only on building the features that are absolutely necessary to prove the main value of the B2B solution and solve the customer's specific business problem. Avoid building features “for the future”, elaborate user roles or advanced admin panels, which lengthen development time and draw attention away from verifying the main hypothesis.
Link an existing Goal or create a Goal of the “Build result” type. It could read: “Delivering a minimum version of the B2B invoice automation module without unnecessary integrations”. Assign the person technically responsible, agree on a deadline and name the expected proof, that is the evidence of completion. In this case the proof will be a screen recording or a demo of the working main mechanism and a link to the working version.
Agree in the team on the boundaries of the minimum version: if a feature doesn't directly affect the customer's decision to test or buy, put it off for later stages. In Vairo, tasks under a shared goal are enough to track the progress of the work.
1.2. Connect the key parts of the solution
After building the individual modules, make sure they come together into a coherent, working business user path (end-to-end). The user has to be able to go through the whole process: from the first login or handing over data, through doing the key business operation, to getting the expected result (e.g. generating a report, sending a notification, processing a file).
Go through the points of contact between components with the person doing the work:
Is the data entered in the first step passed correctly to the next modules?
Do any simplifications (e.g. the startup team doing part of the process by hand in the background – the so-called Wizard of Oz) break the flow from the B2B customer's perspective?
In the goal card (proof), put the scenario of going through the path and material confirming that all parts work together as a coherent product.
1.3. Make the MVP available for testing
Don't keep the product inside the team and don't drag out internal tests. Bring the minimum version of the solution into the customers' real operating environment. Putting the MVP in the hands of real business users is the only way to check how the app behaves in real working conditions, with the real procedures and constraints of the customer's company.
Prepare a stable test instance (a production or staging environment with isolated data). Make sure access for the first companies is configured and confidential test data doesn't get mixed between them.
As proof, keep the address of the shared version, the list of test access granted and confirmation that the environment is up and ready to accept external users.

2.1. Define the research group and set the study period
Choose the companies and specific people (roles in the organization, e.g. managers, specialists) who best represent your target group of B2B customers. They should be organizations that feel the problem directly and are looking for a solution to it.
Then set a clear time frame for the pilot/test:
Too short a time (e.g. 2 days) won't let users build the tool into their daily routine and won't show the real level of use.
Too long a period without a set end dilutes commitment and delays collecting conclusions. The optimal B2B pilot period is usually 2 to 4 weeks.
Link a Goal of the “Test result” type. In the description, write down the criteria for choosing companies (ideal customer profiles - ICP), the list of qualified organizations and the start and end dates of the study.
2.2. Make the MVP available to users and observe their reactions
Give the chosen research group access to the solution together with the simplest, most concise onboarding instructions possible (e.g. a short onboarding video or a 1-page PDF guide). Getting started with the product has to create as little friction as possible.
During the test period, actively observe users' behaviour:
Track product analytics: which features are used every day, which were used only once and which are completely ignored.
Note the places where users got stuck or needed help from the support team. Objective usage data is much more reliable than later verbal statements during interviews.
As proof, attach a user activity report from the test period (e.g. from an analytics tool or an event log) showing the frequency of logins and the use of individual modules.
Choose people suitable for testing the solution. Choose the companies or people who best represent your target group of B2B customers and really face the problem you're solving.

b2b/b2b-zbierz-feedback.title: Collect feedback
b2b/b2b-zbierz-feedback.guide_body:
3.1. Collect users' opinions and consult the solution with experts
After the set test period, hold structured conversations (evaluation interviews) or send short surveys to the people who tested the MVP. B2B interviews should cover both the people doing the work in the tool (end users) and the people making the financial decisions (decision-makers/buyers).
In parallel, consult the solution with independent industry experts, advisors or experienced B2B entrepreneurs. Experts can point out systemic risks, legal issues, security requirements or integration barriers that an ordinary end user may not notice.
Link a Goal about collecting evaluation information. In the proof, attach recordings/notes from the user interviews and a summary of the opinions obtained from industry experts.
3.2. Collect information about problems and users' expectations
Create one organized register (e.g. a document or a dedicated board) in which all the qualitative feedback is collected, divided into two categorical groups:
Register of errors and barriers: technical mistakes (bugs), interface (UX) errors, moments of confusion, slow performance and places that are unclear to the user.
Register of wishes and expectations (Feature Requests): all suggestions for new features, changes to existing processes or integrations with other business systems used in the customer's company.
The person doing the work and the person responsible for the product should make sure each reported defect has its context assigned (in which company and during which operation it occurred).
As proof, attach a complete document containing the aggregated list of barriers and the development suggestions reported.
b2b/b2b-zbierz-feedback/zbieraj-opinie-u: Get direct information about experiences with the MVP. Hold conversations, surveys or short interviews to learn users' subjective impressions and find out directly what they liked and what caused difficulty.

Get direct information about experiences with the MVP. Hold conversations, surveys or short interviews to learn users' subjective impressions and find out directly what they liked and what caused difficulty. Link the goal required in this point and add the proof in the goal card.
b2b/b2b-zbierz-feedback/konsultuj-rozwia: Seek the opinion of people with the right knowledge or experience. Consult industry experts or experienced entrepreneurs who will look at the solution from a broader perspective and help catch risks invisible to users.

b2b/b2b-przeanalizuj-feedback.title: Analyze the feedback
b2b/b2b-przeanalizuj-feedback.guide_body:
4.1. Assess the level of satisfaction and analyze the reported problems
Move from the collected data to drawing conclusions. Assess users' overall satisfaction using simple qualitative and quantitative indicators (e.g. NPS – Net Promoter Score, a rating of the tool's usefulness on a 1-5 scale or the Customer Effort Score).
Then group the collected defects and barriers:
Count how often individual problems occur (which error affected 80% of users and which was a one-off incident).
Determine the severity of the error: whether the problem blocks getting the main value or is only a minor visual inconvenience.
Write down the result of prioritizing the errors in the goal card, pointing out the defects with the highest impact on B2B customers' satisfaction.
4.2. Analyze the needs regarding features and draw the most important conclusions
Split the reported wishes for new features into two categories:
Critical features (Must-have): elements without which a B2B customer won't decide to buy or keep using the app (e.g. a requirement for a specific integration or data export to PDF/XLS).
Extras (Nice-to-have): features that make work easier but have no key impact on the business decision and the main value.
Set the knowledge gained against the startup's original business assumptions. Prepare a summary laid out as:
What was confirmed (which hypotheses turned out true).
What was undermined / disproved (which market assumptions turned out wrong).
What remains unknown and requires further tests.
Paste into the proof a document with the synthesis of the analysis and a list of the confirmed and disproved business assumptions.

b2b/b2b-okresl-kierunek-dalszego-dzialan: Define the direction of further action

5.1. Set the most important fixes and plan the improvement of the MVP
Based on the analysis, choose a limited set of the highest-priority fixes. Instead of trying to implement all users' whims at once, focus on the changes that will bring the biggest increase in value and remove the main sales blockers.
Prepare a realistic, time-bound plan of fixes (a fix roadmap):
The specific changes to the code or the interface.
The order of implementation (the sequence of changes).
The estimated time for the technical team to make the fixes.
Link a Goal of the “Build result” type for the planned iteration. Attach the approved MVP improvement plan with a defined scope of work.
5.2. Consider changing the assumptions and decide on further action
Analyze whether the scale of negative feedback, low engagement or critical remarks from experts require changing the strategy so far (Pivot).
Assess the need for change in the areas of:
The business model (e.g. a change from a subscription to a usage fee).
The target group (e.g. moving from small companies to medium-sized enterprises).
The main feature / value proposition (shifting the weight to another module of the app).
Based on hard data, make one of three strategic decisions:
Continue and develop: continuing work in the current direction and moving to new tests after the fixes are implemented.
Pivot: a formal change of strategy, model or target group and redesigning the MVP's assumptions.
End the project (Kill): deliberately closing work on the solution if the tests showed no real demand or economic unviability.
Record the chosen strategic decision with its justification in the summary card in Vairo.

Choose the changes with the greatest impact on the product's value. From the conclusions, choose the changes that will bring users the greatest benefit, instead of trying to introduce everything at once.

Choose the changes with the greatest impact on the product's value. From the conclusions, choose the changes that will bring users the greatest benefit, instead of trying to introduce everything at once. Link the goal required in this point and add the proof in the goal card.
Plan the improvement of the MVP
Decide how to adapt the solution to the feedback received. Create a specific, realistic action plan describing what changes will be made, in what order and in what time.

Decide how to adapt the solution to the feedback received. Create a specific, realistic action plan describing what changes will be made, in what order and in what time. Link the goal required in this point and add the proof in the goal card.

Assess whether a partial or complete change of direction is needed. Consider whether the test results point to the need for a pivot — a change of the business model, the target group or the product's main feature.

Assess whether a partial or complete change of direction is needed. Consider whether the test results point to the need for a pivot — a change of the business model, the target group or the product's main feature.

Choose further development, a pivot or ending the project. Based on the collected data, decide deliberately whether to continue development in the current direction, change the strategy or end the project — what do you choose?
Choose the direction of work. To pause or archive the startup, end the stage with the pause or archive decision — the answer alone won't do it.
6.1. Introduce the most important changes and make the solution available to users again
Do the development and configuration work according to the prepared fix plan. Implement the chosen changes in the product, keeping the whole path coherent and without breaking features that worked correctly before.
Then make the improved version of the MVP available to users again:
First, give the updated version to the same companies that reported the earlier problems, to check whether the change meets their needs.
If needed, extend the group with a few new B2B organizations to verify that the results are repeatable.
As proof, attach a description of the changes made (Changelog / Version 1.1) and confirmation that the updated environment has been made available to the test group.
6.2. Compare the results before and after the changes and repeat the validation process
Take new measurements and collect opinions from users using the changed version of the product.
Set the results of both research rounds directly against each other:
Quantitatively: did the frequency of logins, the time spent in the app or the completion rate of the key path increase? Did the number of error reports drop?
Qualitatively: do users confirm that the previously reported defects and barriers were effectively removed?
Treat validation as a repeatable, continuous cycle of improvements (the Kolb cycle / the Build-Measure-Learn loop). After each round of changes, go back to measuring, analyzing conclusions and deciding on further iterations.
When the results of the second round of tests confirm the B2B product is ready and the key barriers have been eliminated, choose the status “Version ready for first use / commercialization” in the Vairo tracking system. The stage is closed according to the platform's general guidelines once the conditions for the required proofs are met.

b2c.title: B2C
b2c.intro: A layer for consumer products — making it available, testing, fixes.
b2c/b2c-przetestuj-pozyskiwanie-uzytkown:
1.1. Launch paid acquisition campaigns and measure the conversion rate and the cost of acquisition (CAC)
Open the prepared marketing materials and budget assumptions for the first version of the B2C product. Choose the basic channels for reaching people (e.g. ads on social media or in a search engine) and launch paid campaigns with a small, controlled test budget. The goal isn't to scale sales yet, but to bring the first group of real users from the target group to the website or the app and check whether the prepared message generates genuine interest.
Link an existing Goal or create a Goal of the “Test result” type. It could read: “Launching a $120 test campaign, bringing in the first 1,000 visitors and measuring conversion”. Assign the person responsible for marketing or growth, agree on the duration of the test and name the expected proof, that is the evidence of completion. In this sub-point the proof should be a report from the ad dashboard and from the site's analytics tool (e.g. Google Analytics, PostHog) containing the spending, the number of clicks, the number of add-to-carts and of final purchases.
Analyze the indicators obtained:
Conversion rate: what percentage of unique visitors to the site completed a purchase or created a free account.
Customer acquisition cost (CAC): divide the total amount spent on ads by the number of paying customers acquired in this period.
The person responsible for the Goal has to make sure the analytics correctly count purchase events (the so-called Pixel or Conversion API). Record the calculated CAC and conversion rate in the result description. Use the collected data as a reference point for further optimization attempts.
1.2. Find and remove bottlenecks and optimize the creatives and messages
When the first data comes in from the campaign, look at the whole path the user takes from seeing the ad to completing the purchase. The first version of a funnel rarely works optimally. Use product analytics and session recording tools (e.g. Hotjar, Clarity, PostHog) to locate exactly the moments when users leave the site en masse or abandon the purchase.
Analyze the points of resistance identified (bottlenecks):
Does the page load fast enough on mobile devices?
Does the headline on the landing page directly refer to the promise from the ad?
Does the order or sign-up form require too many unnecessary fields?
Are the pricing and the delivery/subscription costs simple and clear?
Based on the conclusions from the analytics, prepare hypotheses for A/B tests. Change single elements: test different headlines, other images or videos in the ads, more direct call-to-action (CTA) buttons or a modified offer structure. Don't make all the changes at once, because you won't know which change brought the improvement.
Run another campaign test with the chosen variants. In the proof in the goal card, attach a “before and after” comparison of the results – showing how changing the messages or removing an obstacle lowered the CAC and raised the conversion rate.
Release the prepared ads with a small budget to bring the first group of real users to the site and check whether the ads generate interest.

Release the prepared ads with a small budget to bring the first group of real users to the site and check whether the ads generate interest. Link the goal required in this point and add the proof in the goal card.

Check what percentage of visitors make a purchase and how much acquiring one paying customer costs on average. Link the goal required in this point and add the proof in the goal card.

b2c/b2c-ocen-zaangazowanie-i-utrzymanie-:
2.1. Measure the level of return to the product (Retention) and analyze activity in the referral program
Acquiring a customer is only the beginning of the road in the B2C model. It's just as important to check whether the user actually uses the purchased product or app and whether they come back to it after the first contact. Prepare and analyze the return rates (Retention Rate) 1, 7 and 30 days after purchase or sign-up.
Set up retention tracking in the analytics dashboard:
Day 1 Retention: how many users open the app or come back to the platform the next day?
Day 7 and Day 30 Retention: what share of customers still actively use the service after a week and after a month?
If a viral mechanism or a referral program is planned in the product, check how it really works. Measure how many users generate and share their unique referral link and what percentage of the people invited through it actually create an account or make a purchase.
Link a Goal of the “Test result” type covering the analysis of retention and referrals. In the proof, paste the retention cohort summary from the analytics and the referral program statistics. If retention drops drastically after the first day, it's a signal that the onboarding process itself (the introduction to the product) or the initial value needs improving.
2.2. Identify the moment of key value (Aha! Moment) and examine the reasons for cancelling (Churn)
To build retention, you have to know exactly which action in the product gives the user the fastest sense of benefit. This is the so-called Moment of Key Value (or Aha! Moment) – a specific action after which the chance that the user stays with the product for good rises drastically.
Capturing and analyzing these behaviours requires combining data and conversations:
Analyze the behaviour data of returning customers (e.g. “users who added at least 3 friends or created their first playlist within the first 24h have an 80% higher D30 Retention”).
Identify this key action and set up onboarding so that it gets every new user to it as quickly as possible.
In parallel, collect and analyze data on cancellations (Churn). Contact directly (by email, by phone or through an exit survey) the people who cancelled their subscription, stopped opening the app or asked for a refund. Ask directly what the main reason for leaving was (e.g. lack of time, too high a price, not understanding the features, technical errors).
Record the identified Aha! Moment and the list of the most common reasons for cancelling in the goal summary. This information will be key for the product and marketing team to make fixes before scaling.

b2c/b2c-obsluz-zwroty-reklamacje-i-kwest: Handle returns, complaints and legal matters

3.1. Measure the return rate and launch abandoned cart recovery
Analyze transactions in terms of returns, complaints and unfinished purchases. Reacting quickly to signs of dissatisfaction and catching "abandoned opportunities" helps secure the startup's revenue.
Actions to take in this area:
Handling and measuring returns: keep an ongoing record of refund requests. Calculate the refund rate as the ratio of the number of refunds to the total number of transactions. Categorize each request by reason (e.g. “product not as described”, “payment problem”, “customer changed their mind”).
Abandoned cart recovery: build and launch automatic reminder sequences (e.g. email, SMS or push) aimed at people who gave their contact details or started the purchase process but didn't complete the payment. Check whether the emails go out at the right time (e.g. after 1 hour, after 24 hours) and whether they contain a direct link to finish the transaction.
Link a Goal of the “Build result” or “Test result” type. Attach to the proof the total return rate with the list of reasons and screenshots / a report from the working automatic cart recovery system showing the share of recovered sales.
3.2. Take care of legal consents and GDPR
Before you increase ad budgets and start collecting data on a large scale, make sure the whole legal layer and the collection of personal data in the B2C product fully comply with the regulations (including GDPR, the Omnibus directive, consumer law).
Check the following areas with a specialist or based on verified templates:
Collecting emails and marketing consents: are the checkboxes under the sign-up and newsletter forms voluntary, unticked by default and do they contain a correct information clause?
Analytics and cookies: does the cookie banner (Cookiebot/CMP) block tracking scripts (e.g. Meta Pixel, Google Analytics) from loading until the user gives explicit consent?
Terms of service and privacy policy: do the terms of sale/service clearly define the conditions of the service, the right to withdraw from the contract within 14 days, the complaint procedure and the company's full registration details?
Attach to the proof links to the published terms of service and privacy policy and a screenshot of the correctly configured cookie banner with the consent mode checked.
Calculate what percentage of customers ask for a refund and record the specific reasons, so you know which problems need fixing.

Calculate what percentage of customers ask for a refund and record the specific reasons, so you know which problems need fixing. Link the goal required in this point and add the proof in the goal card.

b2c/b2c-przeprowadz-poglebione-wywiady-z:
4.1. Talk to paying customers and collect the reasons for not buying from non-paying ones
Quantitative data from analytics shows what users do, but only direct qualitative conversations explain why they behave that way. Hold interviews with two different groups of recipients:
Paying customers: contact a few people who made a purchase. Have short conversations with them (e.g. 15-20 min on Google Meet). Find out:
What main problem or need brought them to your product?
What exactly in the message or the product itself convinced them to take out their card and pay?
What other solutions did they consider before?
Visitors who didn't buy: contact people who spent time on the site, signed up for a trial or left the cart but didn't make a purchase. Ask in a non-judgmental tone:
What made them decide not to buy at that moment?
What concerns, doubts or barriers stopped them at the last stretch (e.g. an unclear offer, too high a price, lack of trust)?
Record the key quotes, conclusions and recurring patterns from these conversations in a separate Vairo document or note.
4.2. Get reviews and social proof
Trust is a key factor affecting conversion in the B2C segment. The first positive experiences and reviews from real customers are the most effective tool for overcoming the concerns of further visitors.
Actions to take:
Ask the first satisfied, paying users for a short review, a star rating or a statement (testimonial).
Get their formal consent to use their image/name/profile name and their statements in marketing materials.
Put the reviews, references or rating widgets you got directly on the landing page, in the sales funnels and in the cart recovery emails.
In the proof in the goal card, link to the page containing the updated social proof sections and a summary of the references obtained.
Have conversations with the people who bought the product and find out what problem they wanted to solve and what convinced them to pay.

b2c/b2c-potwierdz-oplacalnosc-biznesu-i-: Confirm the business is profitable and set the next step

5.1. Set the cost of acquisition (CAC) against customer value (LTV), reach the MVP goal and decide (Scale or Pivot)
This is the moment of summing up the whole Execution stage for B2C. Based on all the collected proofs, measurements and interviews, you have to assess the product's business potential and decide on the startup's next steps.
Key assessment steps:
Setting CAC against LTV: compare the average cost of acquiring a customer (CAC from point 1.1) with the expected or actual customer lifetime value (LTV – Lifetime Value). In subscription models, LTV is estimated from the average customer retention period and the monthly fee. A sustainable B2C model usually requires LTV to be at least 3 times higher than CAC ($LTV \ge 3 \times CAC$).
Validating the MVP's quantitative assumption: check whether the startup has won the number of paying customers set at the start of the validation stage (e.g. the first 50 or 100 paying users).
Strategic decision (Scaling vs Improvement/Pivot):
Scaling: if $CAC$ is safely low, retention is stable, and the return rate and churn are under control – decide to increase ad budgets and scale the acquisition channels.
Improvement / Pivot: if acquiring a customer is too expensive ($CAC > LTV$), customers cancel en masse after a few days and the return rate is high – stop increasing ad budgets. Focus on improving the product's value, rebuilding the offer or changing the target group.
State the decision made and attach all the proofs from sub-points 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, 3.1, 3.2, 4.1 and 4.2. If the validation conditions have been met and the business shows potential profitability, choose the option confirming “Version ready for first use / scaling” in the tracking system.
